newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli survives African sky, sea hijack drama.
newsitem.headline: Israeli survives African sky, sea hijack drama.

text.p: An Israeli passenger thrown into the sea during the crash of a hijacked Ethiopian airliner said on Sunday he managed to rescue a woman and her baby from the airplane wreckage after extricating himself.

"We simply went into an emergency landing in the sea and I felt a powerful shaking. I was thrown from the seat, and water penetrated the plane, and somehow I managed to get out. I don't know how," Lior Fox, 23, told Israel Radio.

Fox, one of 52 passengers and crew to survive the crash of the Boeing 767, spoke by telephone from a hospital bed in Comoro Islands where he was recovering from back pains. The plane on Saturday crashed into the Indian Ocean just off one of the islands that make up the archipelago.

Having recently completed his mandatory army service in a combat unit, Fox was taking an extended African holiday -- common among Israelis just out of the army -- when he found himself caught in an air piracy drama.

Before the crash, as the plane was running out of fuel, the pilot informed passengers one engine was no longer working and the second would soon go out as well. Fox said it was clear they were going to crash into the sea.

He and an Israeli travelling companion had made plans to fling open the doors and lead the people out. But Fox said he didn't see his friend from the moment they crash-landed and the plane began filling up with water.

"I saw a woman with a baby who was caught, and I swam towards her and freed them from the wreckage and inflated the life preserver for her, and for the baby I inflated the life preserver, and we got up together on a boat," Fox said.
He said it was a good thing his own life preserver flew off his neck from the impact of the crash.

"That's what saved me in essence because it enabled me to free myself from the junk that was holding me and I managed somehow to get out of the water. If I had the life preserver on me, I would have remained there in the ruins," he said.
Fox, one of eight Israelis aboard the plane, said so far as he knew there were three Ethiopian hijackers. They said they were from the Ethiopian opposition and had just been freed from prison.

"The whole time they concentrated on the cockpit and after a quarter hour of flight they removed the deputy pilot from the cockpit and stayed with him (the pilot) alone. One of them claimed he had a grenade in his hand.

"He said that if anyone tries anything, he will set off the grenade immediately and on the spot. He spoke three languages -- English, French and Amharic and he claimed they were from the opposition and they were just freed from prison.

"Aside from that he didn't tell the crew of any destination, he didn't tell the passengers of any destination, but simply continued to fly until the fuel ran out," Fox said. Most of the survivors were from the rear part of the plane, he said.

During an emotional phone interview broadcast live by the radio, Fox tried to reassure his mother Yvette Fox, telling her: "Everything's ok, be calm, I'm ok, Mom." When asked by Uri Fox, his father, if he would be able to make it home on his own, the son said: "I will be able to, maybe lying down."
